subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: Monaco is better equipped than most. Dr. Barrueta is named on the homepage — a named cosmetic doctor is the strongest trust signal an aesthetic practice can publish, and most never do it. The navigation carries Before & After, Financing and Reviews, which are the three things a hesitating patient actually goes looking for. The phone number and a Book Now button both sit in the header.

On a phone, none of that survives the first screen. Every line of the headline runs off the right edge — “Monaco M…”, “Midtown M…”, “Where A Passion…”, “Aesthetic…” — and the subheading naming Dr. Barrueta is cut off before his name appears. A search field also sits over the Book Now button in the header, with a second Book Now beneath it.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on desktop and mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The assets here are genuinely strong — nearly all the score lost is lost to how the first screen renders on a phone.

scorecard.finding: Every headline line is cut off at the right edge on mobile.
A named cosmetic doctor — whose name is cut off on a phone.
Book Now, phone and Financing all present; the header overlaps on mobile.
Before & After and Reviews are in the menu, not near the decision.
Headline overflow and overlapping header controls.
Midtown Miami named, phone number in the header.

strengthsLead: Several of these are things we spend most reports recommending to other practices. They are already here.

strengths.title: The cosmetic doctor is named on the homepage.
strengths.body: “…staffed by the Best Cosmetic Doctor in Miami: Dr. Barrueta”. Naming the doctor is the single most valuable trust signal in aesthetics, and the majority of practices we review never do it at all.

strengths.title: Financing is in the main navigation.
strengths.body: Answering the price objection before it is raised, rather than waiting for a patient to ask and hoping. Very few practices give it a menu item, and for higher-ticket treatment plans it removes a real barrier.

strengths.title: Before & After has its own section.
strengths.body: It is the first thing an aesthetic patient looks for and the hardest to fake. Giving it a navigation item rather than burying it inside a treatment page is the right call.

strengths.title: Phone, booking and reviews are all in reach.
strengths.body: “Call 786-536-6117” top left, a Book Now button top right, and Reviews in the menu. A visitor has several routes forward and none of them is hidden.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The full headline is readable, Dr. Barrueta is named in the subheading, and the navigation carries Before & After, Financing and Reviews.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. Every headline line runs off the right edge, the doctor's name is cut off, and a search field sits over the Book Now button.

findings.heading: The whole headline runs off the side of the screen.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the hero reads “Monaco M”, “Midtown M”, “Where A Passion”, “Aesthetic” — every line clipped at the right margin. The subheading is cut at “The Best Med Spa in Mi…” and “Cosmetic Doctor in M…”, so Dr. Barrueta's name never appears on the screen at all.
findings.why: The largest text on the site is unreadable on the device most patients use, and the casualty is the practice's best asset. A named doctor is the reason a full-fee patient chooses one clinic over another — and on a phone that name is off-screen.
findings.recommended: Reduce the headline size at phone widths so the text wraps inside the viewport rather than overflowing it. One mobile styling rule usually corrects every line at once.

findings.heading: The header controls sit on top of each other.
findings.evidence: On mobile a white search field overlays the header, covering the first Book Now button, with a second Book Now button appearing below it. Two booking controls and a search box occupy the same space.
findings.why: The first thing a visitor sees is controls colliding, and the booking button — the one thing the practice wants pressed — is the element being covered.
findings.recommended: Collapse the search into the menu on narrow screens and keep a single Book Now button in the header. Search is rarely used on a clinic homepage; booking always is.

findings.heading: Two superlatives in one sentence.
findings.evidence: The subheading reads “The Best Med Spa in Miami staffed by the Best Cosmetic Doctor in Miami: Dr. Barrueta”.
findings.why: A sceptical patient discounts claims a practice makes about itself, and doubling them halves rather than doubles the effect. The genuinely persuasive part of that sentence is the last two words — a named doctor — and it is currently doing the least work because it arrives after two unverifiable claims. Superlative claims in medical advertising are also an area where rules vary by state and warrant professional review; that is a question for your own adviser rather than this report.
findings.recommended: Lead with the doctor and his qualification, and let the credential replace the adjectives. “Cosmetic treatments led by Dr. Barrueta” is stronger than “the best” precisely because it can be checked.

findings.heading: A grammatical slip in the largest text on the site.
findings.evidence: The headline reads “Where A Passion For Beauty And Aesthetics Meet!” — a singular subject with a plural verb. Every word is also capitalised.
findings.why: It is small, and on the biggest words on the page it is the kind of thing a careful reader notices without being able to say why the site feels less polished. For a practice whose subheading claims to be the best in the city, precision in the sentence above it matters.
findings.recommended: “Where a passion for beauty and aesthetics meets” — and set it in sentence case, which reads faster than title case at large sizes.

findings.heading: The hero photograph sits in a different register to the offer.
findings.evidence: The hero is a full-bleed image of a woman in a black bikini reclining on a lounger, lit and cropped to emphasise the body, occupying the whole first screen behind the headline.
findings.why: This is a commercial observation rather than a matter of taste. The subheading below it leads with a cosmetic doctor — a clinical proposition — while the image reads closer to lifestyle or resort photography. A patient researching injectables is making a medical decision and looking for clinical confidence, and the two signals pull against each other. Practices that show their own room, team or results generally hold that patient more effectively.
findings.recommended: Consider the practice's own premises, Dr. Barrueta at work, or a genuine before-and-after as the hero. The Before & After material already exists on the site and would do more work here than a stock lifestyle image.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Desktop follows convention well. On mobile, overlapping header controls break the pattern immediately.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Book Now is a good size — the difficulty is that a search field is sitting on top of one of the two copies of it.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: Reviews and Before & After are in the menu rather than beside the booking button, so they reach only the visitors who go looking.
Strong on desktop — a named cosmetic doctor. On mobile his name is cut off the screen.
Two Book Now buttons and a search field compete on mobile, so the single clear action becomes three.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Putting Financing in the navigation is a genuinely helpful default — it answers the unasked question early.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: Two “best in Miami” claims in one sentence is the least believable moment on the page. The named doctor beside them is the most.

roadmap.actions: Fix the headline overflow at phone widths so Dr. Barrueta's name reaches the screen. Collapse search into the menu and keep one Book Now button. Correct the headline grammar.
Lead the subheading with the doctor and his qualification instead of the superlatives. Bring a rating and one before-and-after beside the booking button. Consider clinical imagery for the hero.

Build authority content around Dr. Barrueta. Expand Before & After with consistent lighting and consent. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). The mobile faults were observed at 390 pixels wide and may render differently on other devices. Nothing in this report constitutes advertising, regulatory or legal advice.
